title_en: Is paid antivirus actually a waste of money for your PC in 2026?
title_fa: Is paid antivirus actually a waste of money for your PC in 2026?
excerpt_en: Subscribing to an antivirus suite kept you safe a long time ago, but they're much less useful for most people today.
excerpt_fa: Subscribing to an antivirus suite kept you safe a long time ago, but they're much less useful for most people today.
content_en:
Is paid antivirus actually a waste of money for your PC in 2026?
Windows has great protection built-in, so third-party suites come down to the extras.
Windows was not the safest operating system in the early days. Back then, malware and viruses were a risk that you were required to avoid and resolve on your own. As attacks grew, a whole antivirus industry spun up to provide protection for millions of PC users. Suites like McAfee, AVG and Norton were common options people installed to keep their computers safe.
Times have moved on, though. We've had built-in antivirus protection on PCs since Windows 8 launched in 2012. But third-party antivirus software still exists, along with apps offering more complex anti-malware protection. While there can be uses for these other tools, protection is now baked into your PC from the first day you boot, so you don't need to pay for it.
Windows' built-in antivirus protection is now pretty good
It took a few years for Microsoft Defender Antivirus to become something you can rely on. If you roll back 11 years and look at AV-Test's May–June 2015 testing, Defender scored just 0.5 out of six for the quality of its protection. Compare that to results from July-August 2026, where Defender earned the full six point. It detected 100 percent of threats in both the real-world attack and widespread malware tests, compared with industry averages of 99.9 percent and 100 percent each. Independent testing doesn't guarantee you'll have the same experience, but these real-world scenarios give you an idea of how Defender will react to threats your PC might face.
In Windows 11, Microsoft Defender Antivirus is a core part of the Windows Security suite. It'll scan your PC automatically, checking files and apps as you access them. Regular security updates mean you won't have to remember to download new malware definitions, either.
Defender will work in the background, but if you need to scan a file on-demand right-click it, choose Show more options if necessary, then hit Scan with Microsoft Defender. You're able to check for more threats in the Windows Security app by Virus & threat protection > Quick scan, with other ways to check for malware under the Scan options section.
Paid security suites can prove useful in some cases
In 2026, true viruses aren't the only (or even most common) threat you'll face on your PC. There are fake login pages designed to steal your passwords, scam emails that tell you to pay an invoice and fake security pop-ups claiming you need to call a phone number because your PC is at risk. All this, and plenty more, tries to trick you into making a mistake.
This is where the modern antivirus industry now lies: extras. Most third-party antivirus software has a free tier for core protection, but that's just one component in wider security subscriptions that offer various layers of protection. Anti-scam tools, VPNs, password managers and more are all bundled in to give you a reason to subscribe. Malwarebytes, for instance, advertises additional ransomware and anti-exploit protection in its paid plan. Norton's 360 Deluxe plan, meanwhile, includes a VPN, parental controls and 50GB of cloud backup storage. These plans often cover the whole family, with apps for smartphones and other devices.
These aren't completely useless; a full security suite could be useful if you're helping someone who struggles to spot scams and other online dangers. Those additional warnings and blocks can help, and the additional security layers of a VPN (if it's good enough) can also help protect your data online, especially if blocks ads and trackers.
The question is whether you'll actually use what's included, and a lot of people will likely not. Malwarebytes' free app is good as a second-opinion scanner; combined with 24/7 Microsoft Defender protection, you don't need to pay an extra cent to have a solid level of coverage on your PC. If you want to use tools like a VPN or password manager, you'll find dedicated, more reliable options. Our Norton VPN review found it lacking compared to others, for instance.
Your browser likely has additional protection built-in for free. Microsoft Edge, for example, has SmartScreen protection, which automatically checks websites you visit for any reports of phishing or malware. It'll also warn you about potentially dangerous downloads. It's an important reminder that security software is only one of the pillars of online safety.
Don't keep paying for antivirus software out of habit
If you've been using PCs for decades, subscribing to an antivirus program might feel like something you're supposed to do. That was understandable when Windows had little built-in protection, but it's time to reconsider. If you pay for a full security suite, how many of those extras have you actually used? Browser add-ons and maintenance utilities add bloat to your system.
The free versions of third-party AV tools can also be a pain. Constant pop-ups about minor issues or prompts to upgrade make the software feel like an ongoing sales pitch. These companies need paid subscribers, while Microsoft has a clear interest in keeping Windows safe by default. That's why Microsoft Defender Antivirus doesn't nag you unless there's a problem. You can't run both, either. Installing a third-party antivirus with real-time protection usually results in Defender switching itself off to keep conflicts at a minimum.
You'll also need to think about performance. Third-party antivirus software isn't going to automatically slow down your PC, but Tom's Guide found that running a full scan with Malwarebytes Premium dropped Cyberpunk 2077's performance down from 87 to 75 fps on its test PC. Bitdefender had a smaller impact, dropping from 100 to 97 fps during a full scan.

title_en: Rivian’s CEO says autonomy will enable ‘dramatically different’ vehicle designs
title_fa: Rivian’s CEO says autonomy will enable ‘dramatically different’ vehicle designs
excerpt_en: Founder and CEO RJ Scaringe said he thinks autonomy will allow his company to build radically different kinds of vehicles than the outdoorsy SUVs and trucks it currently makes.
excerpt_fa: Founder and CEO RJ Scaringe said he thinks autonomy will allow his company to build radically different kinds of vehicles than the outdoorsy SUVs and trucks it currently makes.
content_en:
Rivian is going full steam ahead on developing autonomous vehicle software for its EVs, to the point that it is willing to delay profitability. Founder and CEO RJ Scaringe said last week at TechCrunch Disrupt that he thinks autonomy will allow his company to build radically different kinds of vehicles than the outdoorsy SUVs and trucks it currently makes.
“Where it gets really interesting is when you think beyond R2 and R3 and start to imagine the form factors that you want to build for a personally owned autonomous vehicle. You know, it opens up all kinds of design opportunities. It can create dramatically different experiences,” he said in an interview with TechCrunch. “I’m wildly excited about what the next 10 years look like in transportation because of what this enables us to dream and think about.”
This is not a new idea, to be sure. A decade ago, autonomous vehicle companies, legacy automakers, and many others promised that autonomy, combined with the proliferation of battery-electric drivetrains (which are simpler and take up less space than their gas-powered predecessors), would produce a Cambrian explosion of new mobility form factors.
This led to all kinds of crazy concepts getting bandied about at the time. Mercedes-Benz touted a bubbly pod-like design, as well as a long sedan packed with tech. Toyota and others dreamed up “rooms on wheels.” Hyundai once even showed off its idea for a car with legs.
This promised design revolution never escaped the concept and prototyping phase. Autonomy took longer than those companies anticipated to develop, and automakers (new and old) struggled with the harsh realities of manufacturing and selling an entirely new category of vehicle.
The difference now is that Scaringe’s comments come at a time when there are real robotaxis roaming the streets of multiple cities around the world. The software that powers them has seemingly developed to a level that is capable enough to operate them safely on public roads at scale, even if there are still some issues to work out when it comes to integrating them into the urban fabric of cars, bikes, pedestrians, and emergency vehicles. The components that make up electric vehicle motors and batteries have gotten cheaper, and companies like Tesla and Rivian (and many more in China) have gotten better at building them at scale.
Rivian has a lot of work ahead before it gets to driverless vehicles. The company is at the beginning of its effort to scale production of the R2 SUV, which it needs to get right in order to reverse years of losses that it incurred to become a major EV player.
On the autonomy side, Rivian is just a few years removed from completely reworking its approach to self-driving software, and it still has a ways to go.
The company has shipped a driver-assistance system that allows drivers to take their hands off the wheel, while still watching the road. It has promised that, by the end of this year, that software will be capable of driving from start to finish — which the company calls “point-to-point navigation” — without intervention, though still under driver supervision. And it is working toward full autonomy, which it plans to deploy in robotaxi versions of its R2 SUV that will be available on Uber’s ride-hail app.
But if Rivian achieves full autonomy, most of that driving will be done in personally owned vehicles, Scaringe said in the interview, echoing previous comments he’s made.
“You know, 95% of the miles driven in the United States — so this is trillions of miles — 95% of these miles are in things that we personally own, so like you own it, or your household owns it. And so our view is it’s unlikely, even with Level 4 capabilities, that we’re going to see a dramatic societal shift away from that,” he said, referencing the Society of Automotive Engineers’ classification for autonomous vehicles that operate in a specific area.
That figure “may go from 95% to 90%, it may go from 95% to 80%, but still the vast majority of the miles driven for a lot of societal and psychological reasons are likely to stay the same,” he said.
It’s this belief that has Scaringe dreaming about the design of a fully autonomous, personally owned Rivian, he said.
As for what that looks like, though, Scaringe was mum.
“So we did R1, then we did R2, then we did R3. The thing after R3 is going to be called R4 — we just haven’t shown what it looks like,” he said. “It’s going to be cool. It’s going to be great.”

title_en: Homeland Security bans DeepSeek use in federal civilian agencies
title_fa: Homeland Security bans DeepSeek use in federal civilian agencies
excerpt_en: The decision comes a couple of days after the release of Deepseek's latest AI model.
excerpt_fa: The decision comes a couple of days after the release of Deepseek's latest AI model.
content_en:
Homeland Security bans DeepSeek use in federal civilian agencies
The decision comes a couple of days after the release of the company’s latest AI model.
The Department of Homeland Security has issued a sweeping restriction to remove DeepSeek use across all federal civilian agencies and their IT systems. In a notice published with the Federal Register, DHS characterized the risks of DeepSeek use as potentially resulting in the "transfer of sensitive data" of US government employees and vendors to the Chinese government.
Following the order, civilian agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency or Federal Communications Commission would have to exclude any DeepSeek products from being used, while also removing any existing related products. DHS said in the notice that DeepSeek's models could "contain malware or other security vulnerabilities." The notice also disallows DeepSeek from participating in any federal government contracts.
DHS' order comes on the heels of DeepSeek releasing its latest model, V4.1-Flash-1017, which the company called "smarter, faster, more efficient." However, it's not the first time that the Chinese AI company has run into friction with the US government, especially at a time when its cheaper AI models start to rival the likes of ChatGPT or Gemini. Last year, two US Congressmembers proposed a bill that would ban DeepSeek's AI chatbot from government devices.

title_en: Amazon to fund 12 small nuclear reactors at former Indiana coal plant
title_fa: Amazon to fund 12 small nuclear reactors at former Indiana coal plant
excerpt_en: Amazon and X-energy have inked another deal to deploy nuclear power to the grid. This one will generate nearly 1 gigawatt of electricity.
excerpt_fa: Amazon and X-energy have inked another deal to deploy nuclear power to the grid. This one will generate nearly 1 gigawatt of electricity.
content_en:
Amazon is funding development of a proposed 960-megawatt nuclear plant in Indiana and would be the first customer to buy its power, the companies announced Monday. Utility company American Electric Power (AEP) would operate the plant. X-energy, which designs small modular nuclear reactors and went public in April, would supply the reactors.
The new power plant would consist of 12 Xe-100 small modular reactors and be located on the site of a demolished coal power plant just south of Terre Haute. The deal is the second commercial agreement between Amazon and X-energy, and it’s three times larger than the first, which was announced two years ago.
Amazon has invested heavily in X-energy, leading a $700 million Series C-1 round in October 2024. The two companies have said they ultimately plan to build 5 gigawatts of new nuclear generating capacity in the U.S. by 2039.
Unlike many newly announced power plants, these reactors would be connected to the public electric grid, though Amazon says the power would also serve its data centers.
The companies’ aggressive timeline still depends on X-energy successfully delivering its first power plant at a Dow Chemical plant southeast of Houston, Texas. The site, called Seadrift, has recently been at the center of a lawsuit filed by the state of Texas, which accuses the plant of “habitual non-compliance” with water and solid-waste regulations and permits.
X-energy has yet to break ground at Seadrift, which will host four Xe-100 reactors to provide the chemical plant with heat and electricity. The company said its construction permit is in the final phases of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s review process.
Startups and large cloud computing companies are betting that small modular reactors (SMRs), like the kind being developed by X-energy, will help pull the nuclear industry out of its slump. The most recent nuclear power plants built in the U.S. suffered from egregious budget overruns and slipped timelines.
By shrinking the reactor, companies like X-energy hope that mass manufacturing will keep costs and schedules in line. Even then, it could be a tall order. Experts say mass manufacturing often doesn’t start producing benefits for about a decade.
X-energy debuted on the Nasdaq in April in an IPO priced at $23 per share. Investor excitement drove the price up 27% in the first day of trading, but shares of the newly public company have dropped by nearly two-thirds since then.
News of the Amazon deal sent X-energy’s shares up about 10% in premarket trading, though they were down by less than 2% at the time of publication.

title_en: At what distance does a video doorbell stop detecting motion?
title_fa: At what distance does a video doorbell stop detecting motion?
excerpt_en: Your video doorbell might see a visitor without sending an alert. Detection depends on more than distance, and some surprising factors can affect its reach.
excerpt_fa: Your video doorbell might see a visitor without sending an alert. Detection depends on more than distance, and some surprising factors can affect its reach.
content_en:
At what distance does a video doorbell stop detecting motion?
Not all video doorbells are made equal.
Just because someone is seen by your video doorbell does not mean that the device will detect them and alert you. Ring says the standard maximum motion detection range for its devices is about 30 feet (9 meters), but if the object is much bigger than a person, such as a car passing by, it can still trigger an alert from farther away.
Still, maximum distances for these products aren't guaranteed. Some companies' video doorbells have much shorter published ranges than Ring, which we'll explore below, and capabilities can fall short of a maximum advertised range depending on a camera's sensitivity, mounting location and surroundings. Someone may be visible during live view, but not trigger a motion event because detection is based on more than what the camera can see. The sensor, camera angle, directional movement and software settings all factor in.
Motion detection range varies by video doorbell
According to eufy, its Video Doorbell can reliably detect horizontal motion up to 15 feet away and vertical motion up to 5 feet away. Arlo lists a maximum motion detection range of 13 feet for its second-generation Video Doorbell, while the Essential wired and wire-free models are listed at 16 feet. According to TELUS, the doorbell's motion sensor works best within 8 feet.
However, it's not just about distance. Even at its most sensitive setting, TELUS says its doorbell's motion sensor requires continuous movement for seven seconds or more to trigger a clip. Ring does not state a single per-model maximum for every current doorbell on its general motion settings page.
Motion detection type is equally as important. On one hand, you have passive infrared (PIR) heat sensors, which are more sensitive to side-to-side movement than motion directly toward or away from the camera. In contrast, Pixel Difference Analysis (PDA) compares one video frame with the next to identify differences. Popular examples of each include the Wyze Duo Cam Doorbell, which uses PIR, while Logitech's Circle View uses PDA. Some cameras, like SimpliSafe video doorbells, combine video analytics with PIR.
More motion range isn't always better
If a device like your 4K Ring doorbell isn't detecting visitors in time, you can adjust its Motion Sensitivity and its detection range up to the maximum limit. Companies like Ring also allow you to establish up to three customizable motion zones per device. Motion zones determine which areas of the camera's field of view should detect for recording motion events.
If your front door is on a busy road, that's an important distinction. Ring says that moving trees, sunlight, reflections and shadows can lead to unwanted alerts, and that large vehicles can trigger a motion alert even beyond a standard range, as we established.
There's a battery tradeoff, as well, for wireless or battery-powered doorbell cameras. Google says its battery-powered Nest Doorbell naturally consumes more power when detecting high-traffic areas like a busy sidewalk. In this event, the device's Activity Zones, or a different camera angle, can reduce unnecessary triggers. Ring recommends mounting its video doorbells 48 inches off the ground.
User experience may differ by subscription. Ring allows customers to receive and respond to motion alerts for free, but viewing recorded video requires a Ring Protect subscription, as do Smart Alerts distinguishing between people, vehicles and packages. The company doesn't say that paying for a subscription makes the physical motion detection range bigger.

title_en: Fiber vs. cable internet: What's the difference between them?
title_fa: Fiber vs. cable internet: What's the difference between them?
excerpt_en: Fiber internet is more modern than cable, but the older technology still works well for today's connection needs.
excerpt_fa: Fiber internet is more modern than cable, but the older technology still works well for today's connection needs.
content_en:
Fiber vs. cable internet: What's the difference between them?
They're both suitable options for today's internet needs, but the right one for you depends on availability and price.
For both internet speed and reliability, fiber-optic and cable connections beat alternatives like DSL and satellite connectivity. Fiber is capable of much faster speeds and better reliability, but cable wins in availability while still keeping speeds fast enough. Depending on what you do online, the differences in speed and latency could result in buffering video streams, slow downloads or jittery connections while gaming online.
Fiber-optic cables transmit information as light through thin strands of glass wrapped in protective layers of plastic. As for cable, data moves through electricity. Cut open a coaxial cable, and you'll find a copper core insulated with metal and plastic layers. While it's convenient for ISPs since it utilizes the same infrastructure used to deliver cable TV, relying on electricity to transfer information makes it prone to interference from extreme weather or moisture.
Much of the time, picking between fiber and cable comes down to whether fiber is available in your area. The Fiber Broadband Association found that over 60 percent of American households had access to fiber connectivity as of September 2025, while 96.9 percent of Americans have access to a fixed broadband service at 100/20 Mbps according to the FCC. If you have a choice, you should know how they differ and what makes the most sense for your home.
Is fiber or cable better for internet?
Fiber connections provide better performance than cable because they support vastly higher bandwidth. They aren't subject to cable's physical limitations, where available bandwidth has to be split between two "lanes" for uploading and downloading. For that reason, fiber is also more reliable than cable during peak usage hours. Cable networks share bandwidth with neighboring households, which is why you might notice slower speeds in the evenings when everyone is at home streaming.
While you might see fiber speeds start around 100 Mbps, it's more common to see entry-level offerings around 300 or 500 Mbps, with plans going much higher. As an example, Ziply Fiber offers plans from 2 Gbps all the way up to a wild 50 Gbps. Unlike cable, fiber internet is symmetrical, meaning the upload and download speeds are the same. If you often upload video, live stream or sync files, this is a big difference.
Many internet providers now opt for a hybrid fiber-coaxial network, where fiber lines connect a neighborhood before using coaxial cables for the final section to homes. While it may not be a true end-to-end fiber solution, you can still get download speeds of 1 Gbps or more this way, though upload speeds will be lower.
The cost of fiber compared to cable
A fiber subscription is not necessarily pricier than cable connectivity, depending on ISP deals and especially when you take upload speeds into account. Take Google Fiber, for example, where the 1 Gbps connection (both up and down) is $70 a month, 3 Gbps is $100/month and 8 Gbps is $150/month. In comparison, Xfinity's hybrid cable internet offers 300 Mbps down for $45/month, 500 Mbps down for $60/month, and 1 Gbps down for $70/month. Those prices are all locked in for five years (with no contract required) and will go up after the term.
For cable plans, you'll need to either use the ISP's all-in-one gateway or purchase your own modem and router separately. Fiber internet requires a dedicated Optical Network Terminal (ONT), a fiber equivalent to a modem which most service providers include with your plan.
In case you still want traditional cable or even a home phone, internet service providers often bundle TV services and phone lines with cable internet so you save more. Meanwhile, if you're not happy with the cable or fiber options available in your area, wireless 5G home internet is another potential route, though it's usually slower and has higher latency than wired solutions.
Regardless of which option you choose, you should know how to prevent your home network from running slowly. A cheap router or poorly optimized settings can result in slow Wi-Fi performance even if your ISP plan is super fast. Connecting with Ethernet sidesteps Wi-Fi's interference issues and reduces latency for real-time uses like gaming and video calls.

title_en: People are using AI to make their smart TVs dumb again
title_fa: People are using AI to make their smart TVs dumb again
excerpt_en: Fed up with ads, tracking, and sluggish interfaces, some smart TV owners are turning to AI agents to strip away bloatware and take back control of their TVs.
excerpt_fa: Fed up with ads, tracking, and sluggish interfaces, some smart TV owners are turning to AI agents to strip away bloatware and take back control of their TVs.
content_en:
The latest use case for AI? Dumbing down your smart TV to get rid of the bloat. A number of developers and vibe coders have recently been sharing solutions for “vibe-coding” your TV to get rid of sponsored ads, speed up the app launcher, redesign the home screen, disable tracking features, and more.
One such solution, called “dumbtv,” describes its mission on its GitHub page thus: “Your TV should do what you paid for: your apps, your HDMI inputs, and nothing else. No ads from the TV itself, no watch tracking, no update you did not ask for.”
Another, “cleanyourtv,” promises to strip the bloatware from any Android TV or Google TV over Wi-Fi, to replace the launcher with one that resembles Apple TV.
While hacking consumer electronics devices to gain more control over their systems is hardly a new idea, the latest advances in AI technology have made such efforts much more accessible to anyone. With smart TVs in particular, the hacks come at a time when people have grown frustrated with being forced to watch ads and put up with their devices surveilling their viewing habits.
Modern smart TVs ship with a technology called automatic content recognition (ACR), which identifies what’s playing on the screen using screenshots, audio clips, or other forms of digital fingerprinting.
If these “dumb TV” hacks become more popular among everyday consumers, they have the potential to disrupt the smart TV ad industry, which profits from selling viewing data to advertisers or using it to display personalized ads on their own interfaces.
As the creator of cleanyourtv, Gathin T., puts it, the idea to clean up the smart TV interface started one afternoon when he got tired of seeing the ads on his parents’ TV set.
“I had Claude Code clean it up over Wi-Fi and build a simple home screen with just their apps on it. I put the prompt on GitHub, tweeted the before and after, and a few thousand people did the same to their own TVs over the next two days. Xiaomi, TCL, Sony, Fire TV, LG, a projector or two,” the developer wrote on a website for donations, linked from the project’s homepage.
The solution doesn’t require gaining root access to the TV, nor does it make it impossible to return to the factory default state, if desired.
Meanwhile, the dumbtv solution has been tested end-to-end on a Fire TV Edition television set and Android/Google TV platforms on TVs from Sony, TCL, Philips, Hisense, Xiaomi, and Shield. To use this hack, the developer, Muzzammil Yasin Sabuwala, suggests pointing your preferred AI agent at the dumbtv repository on GitHub.
Sabuwala said he was motivated to work on dumbtv because he was tired of the ads and not being able to delve directly into the content he wanted to watch. His solution was coded using a combination of Deepseek V4.1 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, he told TechCrunch, and he plans to maintain the GitHub, adding support for more models over time.
Fair warning: All these solutions are works in progress, and various users are now testing them across different TV platforms and suggesting updates and fixes.
However, individuals don’t need to borrow someone else’s work from GitHub to get the job done.
In one newly viral X post, Ryan Doyle explains that he simply sent Claude Code the listing for his TV and asked “Can you hack this?” The agent then talked him through the process, allowing him to remove the ads and bloatware from the TV set, speed up the lagging user interface, and customize his screensaver, he claims.
Doyle then goes on to demonstrate in a video how fast and responsive the new interface is after the AI made the requested changes.
Seeing posts about people “vibe-coding their TVs,” inspired one X user, Mihir Gupta, to try it himself.
“One afternoon with Claude Code: 25 bloat apps disabled, the 192 MB stock launcher replaced with a custom 83 MB one, plus rotating wallpapers,” he wrote.
The end result of these hacks may be mixed, however. Some people have found that Claude wouldn’t respond to their simple suggestions to “hack my TV,” necessitating more complex prompts. Others warned that AI agents could make mistakes, possibly disabling important packages or breaking things in the process. One person even said they bricked their Android TV using Claude, and another got stuck halfway through hacking their Fire TV.
For those wary of using AI to fully hack their TVs, there are existing solutions for customizing Android-based smart TVs, such as home screen replacement apps ATV Launcher, Projectivy Launcher, and FLauncher.

title_en: Apple is set to hold another product event on October 28
title_fa: Apple is set to hold another product event on October 28
excerpt_en: Apple's "Pro and Tell" event is taking place in Los Angeles and will likely feature the first touchscreen Mac.
excerpt_fa: Apple's "Pro and Tell" event is taking place in Los Angeles and will likely feature the first touchscreen Mac.
content_en:
Apple is set to hold another product event on October 28
"Pro and Tell" is taking place in Los Angeles and will likely feature the first touchscreen Mac.
Hot on the heels of its smart home-focused showcase, Apple has confirmed its third product event of the season. The company has invited press and influencers to get the first look at new devices in Los Angeles on October 28. Apple is calling the event "Pro and Tell," according to the invite.
It seems likely that this event (which is said to be an all-day affair) will focus on the Mac and iPad. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reiterated previous reporting that Apple will unveil touchscreen MacBooks, more M6-powered Macs and an iPad mini with an OLED display at the showcase later this month.
Word on the street is that touchscreen MacBooks will have M5 Pro and Max chipsets and be available in 14-inch and 16-inch formats. They're said to be significantly lighter than current Pro models and have OLED displays. It's also expected that Apple will refresh the 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac. Those are slated to run on the M6, which debuted in August in the latest Mac mini.

Apple teases MacBook Pro event next week
Following Apple’s smart home-focused launch earlier in the month, Apple is hosting another product event soon.
Following Apple’s smart home-focused launch earlier in the month, Apple is hosting another product event soon.
At the event, Apple is set to announce new Macs and a refreshed iPad Mini, according to Bloomberg. The big announcement is expected to be a new MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen that’s also lighter and has an iPhone-like Dynamic Island. But Apple is also planning on revealing a 14-inch MacBook Pro and a new iMac with the M6 chip, which was recently introduced with the Mac Mini. Apple’s updated iPad Mini will apparently finally get an OLED screen as well and put the selfie cam on the landscape edge.
“Can’t wait to pro and tell next week,” Apple’s SVP Marketing Greg Joswiak says in a teaser on X.
This second October launch follows Apple’s smart home-focused “Welcome home” event on October 13th, which included the new HomeView smart home hub, an updated Apple TV 4K and Siri Remote, and a second-generation HomePod Mini.

title_en: Why your USB device keeps disconnecting (and how to fix it)
title_fa: Why your USB device keeps disconnecting (and how to fix it)
excerpt_en: If your USB peripheral is on the fritz, it's worth doing some troubleshooting with the port itself. Give these steps a try.
excerpt_fa: If your USB peripheral is on the fritz, it's worth doing some troubleshooting with the port itself. Give these steps a try.
content_en:
Why your USB device keeps disconnecting (and how to fix it)
A USB device that doesn’t stay connected consistently is no use at all.
USB is supposed to be simple: Plug in a device and your computer can interface with it until you decide to eject it. But at times, a device will constantly disconnect, which poses a major problem since nearly all USB devices rely on a consistent connection. Your mouse will stutter, your keyboard will miss half your inputs, your video camera will cut out and file transfers to an external drive won't be able to complete.
When this happens, you'll need to run through some troubleshooting to see if the device, cable, port or even computer is to blame. In many cases, the solution isn't difficult, but it's always best to start with the easiest potential fix: restarting your computer. You don't want to spend time on extended troubleshooting for a temporary bug.
Check the ports and cables
First, you should try to isolate the problem. Try using the same USB device in another USB port, then use a different USB device in the same port. If one accessory has trouble in every port, then something with the device or your computer is likely at fault. If various accessories all start having issues only when connected to a specific port, you can narrow the problem down to that port.
Inspect the USB connector of your device to see if it's super loose, has bent pins or has suffered other damage. Also check the cable itself for any tears in the jacket, extreme bends or similar issues. Damaged cables are much more likely to cut out frequently, so replace any that are removable.
Shine a light into the port in question to see if anything looks out of place in it; debris buildup could be preventing a good connection. Gently use a wooden toothpick (nothing metal) to loosen it. For anything really stuck, use short bursts of canned air to carefully clean the USB port. If the pins inside the port are warped or otherwise blocking a clean insert, you'll likely need to have a professional look at it unless you're comfortable with hardware repairs.
If you're using a USB hub, try bypassing that and connecting directly to the computer to see if there's a difference. Hubs introduce a new point of failure, especially if you connect high-power devices to a basic model that relies on USB for power. For best results, use a powered USB hub that plugs straight into the wall.
On a desktop, it's best to connect long-term devices to the back ports when possible. Those are directly wired to the motherboard and thus have slightly less overhead than the front USB ports that rely on extension cables.
Review computer and driver settings on Windows
Windows has a few options that cut power to USB ports when they're not being used, which can misbehave and shut off a device you're working with. To adjust the first one, right-click the Start button or press Win + X to open the Windows shortcut menu, then choose Device Manager. In that panel, expand the Universal Serial Bus controllers section. One by one, double-click each item under it, switch to the Power Management tab and uncheck Allow the computer to turn off this device to save power. Be sure to save your changes with OK.
Once that's done, type "power plan" into the Start menu and click the Choose a power plan entry that appears. Next, choose Change plan settings next to the one that's currently enabled and select Change advanced power settings from the resulting screen. Finally, in the pop-up that appears, expand USB settings > USB selective suspend setting and change Setting to Disabled. You've now prevented Windows from turning off USB ports to save power, but be aware that Microsoft "strongly recommends" keeping selective suspend enabled.
It's also possible that the driver for your USB ports is outdated or corrupted, though this is unlikely unless you're using a specialized hub. Back in the Device Manager menu, visit the Driver tab for each USB device and click Update Driver to check for newer versions (it likely won't find any). If you've identified a specific port as troublesome, you can try the Uninstall Device button for that one, then reboot to have it reinstall automatically.
It can be difficult to identify which Device Manager entry corresponds to each port on your PC; a quick method is inserting and removing a device while watching the page. If that doesn't help, try the free USBDeview tool. In theory, you could run through them all in succession, but don't disable the one your keyboard or mouse is plugged into, or you'll lose control.
Further USB troubleshooting steps
We've mostly focused on the computer side, but it's also important to check the device you're trying to connect, especially if it doesn't work with any port. It's possible that something like a mouse, external hard drive or similar has failed, particularly if you've just dropped it or it's otherwise gone through a shock (like getting wet).
It's also a possibility that the USB connection is fine, but what you're trying to do isn't supported by that port (or cable). For instance, not all USB-C ports support video, and sometimes only one of several USB-C ports on a given device works for charging. Assuming there are no markings on the USB ports to make sense of, check the product specs to see what each is intended for.
Make sure you're using the right cable for the job, as well. Some are only meant for charging devices and won't carry data. If you can't transfer files between your phone and PC, for instance, try another cable that's equipped for those tasks.
USB ports are available on more than just PCs, where much of the above also applies. If you're troubleshooting a USB port on your router, car, TV or other device, double-check the manual or online guide to see what each is approved for. title_en: Amazon is funding a new nuclear plant in Indiana
title_fa: Amazon is funding a new nuclear plant in Indiana
excerpt_en: Amazon has signed an agreement with X-energy and American Electric Power (AEP) to fund the building of a new nuclear energy facility in Indiana. The proposed plant, which would replace the now defunct coal-fueled Breed Generating Station in Fairbanks, Sullivan County, aims to...
excerpt_fa: Amazon has signed an agreement with X-energy and American Electric Power (AEP) to fund the building of a new nuclear energy facility in Indiana. The proposed plant, which would replace the now defunct coal-fueled Breed Generating Station in Fairbanks, Sullivan County, aims to...
content_en:
Amazon has signed an agreement with X-energy and American Electric Power (AEP) to fund the building of a new nuclear energy facility in Indiana. The proposed plant, which would replace the now defunct coal-fueled Breed Generating Station in Fairbanks, Sullivan County, aims to provide up to 960 megawatts of carbon-free energy for both the regional power grid and Amazon’s data centers.
Amazon is funding a new nuclear plant in Indiana
The proposed nuclear plant would provide 960 megawatts to power the grid — and Amazon’s data centers.
The proposed nuclear plant would provide 960 megawatts to power the grid — and Amazon’s data centers.
No timeline for construction or operation has been announced for the facility, which Amazon says “could” create 1,000 construction jobs and 100 permanent roles. The facility in Indiana is targeting to build 12 Xe-100 SMR’s, an advanced (but unproven) reactor that’s still undergoing development and licensing. These reactors can be cooled using either air, water, or a hybrid solution of both, which Amazon says should allow them to be deployed in water-constrained regions without impacting water demand in local communities.
Indiana also happens to be home to a famously expensive and uncompleted energy project called the Marble Hill Nuclear Power Plant. It was abandoned half-finished in 1983 after $2.5 billion had already been sunk into it, and has been under continued demolition since 2008. Terms for Amazon’s agreement in Fairbanks haven’t been disclosed, so we can’t compare the cost between the facilities.
This marks the second nuclear energy project that Amazon and X-energy are collaborating on, with the collective goal of working with regional utilities to deploy more than 5 gigawatts of new nuclear capacity in the US by 2039. In October last year, Amazon shared an early preview of its first planned nuclear plant, the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility in Washington. That project is similarly set to build 12 advanced reactors and create local jobs, but construction isn’t expected to start until the end of this decade.
Amazon is one of several tech companies, including Meta, Microsoft, and Google, that are exploring their own nuclear energy projects to power AI data centers. Investing in energy grid infrastructure was also one of the commitments that Amazon outlined in a lengthy blog post earlier this month that aimed to sway some of the growing negativity around data center projects, though it’ll be many years before anyone — including Amazon — can reap the benefits of these new facilities.

title_en: Nvidia launches new open models to run agents in the enterprise and on PCs
title_fa: Nvidia launches new open models to run agents in the enterprise and on PCs
excerpt_en: Nvidia is leaning hard into the trend of enterprise companies wanting to run their own open models in their own data centers and also trying to make on-device, private AI agents a thing.
excerpt_fa: Nvidia is leaning hard into the trend of enterprise companies wanting to run their own open models in their own data centers and also trying to make on-device, private AI agents a thing.
content_en:
Nvidia on Thursday launched new open-weight models designed for always-on agents and edge computing.
The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a large, 120-billion-parameter model geared for agents used by the enterprise. While it uses fewer parameters than the Nemotron 3 Ultra model, Nvidia says it can deliver similar accuracy in instruction-following and tool-use tasks.
At the other end of the spectrum, the company also launched two lightweight Bolt models. These are intended to run locally on the new AI PCs (running the Nvidia RTX Spark chip) and workstations running the DGX Spark. Such PCs, aimed at consumers, programmers, and enterprise knowledge workers, are being released right now into the market through partners like Microsoft and Dell.
“Any organization that wants to run agents on Nvidia infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier without having to choose between capability and deployability,” Nvidia’s vice president of Open Models and Software, Kari Briski, wrote in the blog post announcing these models.
Nvidia claims that the Super VL completes tasks faster than competing models from Anthropic and OpenAI (Opus 5, GPT 6.1 Sol, Luna, Astra) when post-trained on specific agentic tasks. These tasks include document intelligence, financial accounting, scientific experimentation, medical insurance claims, and security attack resilience.
While such claims are standard whenever a major tech company announces a new model, Nvidia has backed it up with a list of heavy-hitter companies that it says are using Super VL. These include Skydance, EY, Ramp, Crowdstrike, Perplexity, and Salesforce.
Of course, these aren’t the first open-weight models that Nvidia has released that compete with the proprietary frontier labs — companies that are both its customers and its investments. The GPU giant has an entire family of Nemotron models that do everything from multimodal artificial intelligence to reasoning, coding, math, and enterprise automation.
However, those fast-growing proprietary AI labs are now looking to many other chips and AI system makers beyond Nvidia to power their needs, like AWS’s Trainium and Cerebras, as well as building their own home-grown chips.
So Nvidia is leaning hard into the trend of enterprise companies wanting to run their own open models in their own data centers. “Unlike closed frontier models, organizations can post-train Super VL on their own data, deploy it on their own infrastructure and own what they build,” Briski wrote.
But with the announcement or the smaller, local PC models, it is also trying to push forward the nascent trend of consumer AI assistants. While it seems a new AI assistant is introduced every day by startups and Big Tech alike, privacy-weary consumers may not want to invite such agents so deeply into their lives giving them access to info about their families, health, finances, and so on.
So, while Nvidia hopes to create a new market for itself selling PCs powered by its chips by creating machines that run the models and agents locally, PC users “can delegate everyday projects … without sending those workloads to the cloud,” Briski wrote.
Of the two Bolt models, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a 74-billion parameter model designed for local agentic tasks. It is intended to balance speed with reasoning to handle multistep reasoning, tool calling, and web browsing. The smallest Bolt E4B is aimed at conversational agents.
Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming later this month, Nvidia says.

title_en: TP-Link moves to assemble routers in the US following an import ban
title_fa: TP-Link moves to assemble routers in the US following an import ban
excerpt_en: Routers could start rolling off a Missouri production line as soon as early 2027.
excerpt_fa: Routers could start rolling off a Missouri production line as soon as early 2027.
content_en:
TP-Link moves to assemble routers in the US following an import ban
The company says routers could start rolling off a domestic production line as soon as early 2027.
TP-Link is looking to put routers together in the US after the government banned new foreign-made units from being sold domestically. The company has signed a letter of intent with manufacturer Key Tronic and, pending approval from regulators, TP-Link says stateside assembly of its routers could start at a Mississippi production line as soon as early 2027.
Once things are up and running, Wi-Fi 8 routers are expected to be among the first TP-Link products that Key Tronic assembles. TP-Link claims that the agreement is part of its "long-term effort to accelerate US investment in high-tech manufacturing and job creation, designing and assembling next-generation products for American consumers here on American soil."
The company said it will still have to source components from outside the US. "Many [components] are just not available from a domestic source, and this is not a TP-Link issue," TP-Link's corporate affairs officer Steve Kovsky told PC Mag. "This is an issue for all manufacturers that are trying to onshore manufacturing."
In March, the Federal Communications Commission designated all consumer routers made outside the US as a security risk and banned imports. Retailers were still allowed to sell units that they already had on shelves. In its notice, the FCC said companies could apply for a waiver, but only if they planned to move at least some manufacturing to the US. Several companies have received waivers, though TP-Link is not currently one of them.

title_en: Don't throw away your old USB charging cables — Repurpose them instead
title_fa: Don't throw away your old USB charging cables — Repurpose them instead
excerpt_en: The charger from your three-generations-ago phone can still be useful. Here are several ways to use old cables, both indoors and out.
excerpt_fa: The charger from your three-generations-ago phone can still be useful. Here are several ways to use old cables, both indoors and out.
content_en:
Don't throw away your old USB charging cables — Repurpose them instead
Turn your junk drawer’s tangled pile of old USB cables into useful everyday tools and crafts.
Most of us have a drawer or box where we keep a tangled pile of old USB cables on top of other cables we probably shouldn't be holding on to. Maybe those charging cables came with a phone you upgraded from three models ago, or maybe they were included with headphones, speakers or a printer you no longer own. Whatever the source, these cables pile up faster than most people realize, especially if you tend to grab newer and faster models every so often.
When decluttering, the instinct may be to throw them straight into the trash, but you should really reconsider. A cable that no longer matches your current devices isn't necessarily useless. Many old USB cables still carry a current perfectly well — they just don't fit the connector on your newest phone or laptop. Others may be worn, frayed or missing a connector altogether, but the copper wiring and durable plastic sheathing still have practical value. Using a frayed cable to conduct a current may pose a fire risk, so be sure you know what you're doing before reusing wiring to power something new. Proceed with extreme caution, or use the cable for one of the current-free uses below.
Rather than defaulting to the trash can or the donation box, there are genuinely creative ways to put those cables back to work. Some ideas require nothing more than a pair of scissors and a few minutes; others call for basic tools like wire cutters and a soldering iron if you're comfortable with electronic projects. Either way, the goal is the same: Get more use out of materials you already own before deciding they're destined for a recycling bin.
How to reuse USB cables that still work
Before cutting into any cable, it's worth testing whether it still conducts power. Such a cable doesn't need to get thrown out. It can keep doing exactly what it was designed for, just in a smaller or more specialized role.
Create a dedicated charging station: Gather up your working cables, bundle them near an outlet close to your desk or kitchen counter and label each one by device type. This keeps cables organized and ensures you're not trying to locate a charger every time a phone or tablet runs low. Even if the cable can't fast-charge your phone, it'll still provide a little bit of power while you're making dinner without having to hunt for a charger in another room.
Put together a dedicated travel charging kit: Those spare cables are just what you need when you go on vacation. If you happen to forget one at the airport or in the hotel room, you won't cry over losing the "good cable." Plus, keeping a separate set packed in a small travel bag means you're never scrambling to gather your tech before a vacation or an unexpected trip.
Reuse cables to power small accessories: Those USB cables you no longer use with your phone and tablet can be just what you need to power LED lights behind your monitor or to illuminate a dark desk corner. If you have basic electronic skills, those old cables with working USB connectors can also power small DIY projects, like simple sensors. You'll probably need a soldering iron and some patience, but you can definitely turn a drawer full of cables into something functional.
How to repurpose USB cables for household and craft projects
Even cables that no longer charge anything reliably still have raw materials worth salvaging. Depending on your imagination and your expertise, there are loads of things you can do with those materials.
The copper core makes surprisingly effective garden twine. Once stripped of its outer shielding and inner insulation, the bare or tinned copper strands are pliable enough to gently tie tomato vines to garden stakes, for instance. In a pinch, the entire cable can even be used to tie a tree to a support stake during a storm.
Indoors, intact cables can be repurposed as plant hangers or picture supports. Cut the connectors from both ends, loop the cable around a pot or a frame and secure it with a knot or hook.
Crafters can have so much fun with such cables. Coiling a flexible cable into a tight spiral and gluing it in place creates a simple coaster. Cable segments threaded through holes drilled into drawers can make unconventional handles if they're secured with a knot or washer. You can even turn these cables, especially ones covered in braided nylon, into keychain lanyards or zipper pulls. If you want to take things a step further, you can make keychains for all family members, leaving the USB connector on the cable. Then, you can find matching female USB ends, arrange them on a tiny plank of some sort, and create a distinctive key mount to put by the door.
For artsy folks, there's also the option of stripping the cables and using those to braid some cool-looking bracelets. You could also arrange them on a canvas or a wood board to create wire art, or make a sculpture out of them by using some armature wire to create the shape, et cetera.
Why you should repurpose and recycle
Even with creative reuse, some cables genuinely reach the end of their usefulness. If that's the case for your cables, you should look into recycling rather than throwing them in the trash. USB cables are made primarily of copper and plastics, materials that don't break down quickly in a landfill. The UN's Global E-waste Monitor 2024 found the world generated 69 million tons of e-waste in 2022, yet only 22.3 percent of it was documented as properly collected and recycled.
Repurposing cables helps keep them out of that waste stream longer and reduces the demand for manufacturing new ones. Big retailers like Best Buy and Staples accept old cables and other small electronics for recycling, often at no cost. If a cable is still in good working order but you simply don't need it, you could also donate it to a local school or nonprofit that runs STEM programs where they could use spare...

title_en: One of the rarest GameCube consoles sells for thousands of dollars today
title_fa: One of the rarest GameCube consoles sells for thousands of dollars today
excerpt_en: While the GameCube came in several colors, a few of the most elusive variations command thousands from game collectors.
excerpt_fa: While the GameCube came in several colors, a few of the most elusive variations command thousands from game collectors.
content_en:
One of the rarest GameCube consoles sells for thousands of dollars today
The most exclusive GameCube variations cost collectors a whole lot of cash.
How much would you be willing to spend when buying a GameCube? While you might be able to find a typical Indigo or Jet Black console for a reasonable price, some of the rarest variations will break the bank and are thus for collectors only.
Sure, there are some attainable relics, like the Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness and Donkey Konga bundles. Both of those were basic Platinum Silver consoles with custom-branded faceplates featuring Lugia and DK, respectively. The former was available in the US, while the latter was Japan-only.
But speaking of Japanese releases, some of the rarest GameCube models were only released in the country. This includes the Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles edition, which arrived in a unique color that went beyond the optional cosmetic faceplate. What's more, it sells for thousands of dollars today. For serious collectors, landing one of these units means shelling out a small fortune on the secondary market.
How much is the Crystal Chronicles GameCube worth?
According to eBay sellers and the experts at Consolevariations, the Crystal Chronicles console bundle was limited to 150 units and only available as a prize in a magazine sweepstakes. As an added nod to the well-received RPG, this model was delivered in Crystal White, a cream-like color that sets it apart compared to the more common Pearl White console sold in Europe.
Two of these ultra-rare variants have sold for upwards of $5,000 this year alone, with the most recent sale going for $7,500. Before that, another listing in May sold for just under $7,000. If you're willing to spend top dollar on a piece of Nintendo history, there's currently an unboxed, slightly scuffed listing up for grabs on eBay for $3,750.
It came alongside a Game Boy Player and a copy of Crystal Chronicles. If you're unfamiliar, the Game Boy Player was an add-on that enabled the GameCube to play Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance cartridges on the TV. In North America, the add-on was only available to buy in Jet Black. Other colors were available throughout Japan, with Crystal White being one of the rarest.
There are other rare GameCube consoles, too
The elusive Heineken GameCube is another standout collector's item; it can be found on eBay for as much as $15,500. In 2002, the Dutch brewer ran a sweepstakes on its website, limiting it to 100 units (50 in Indigo and 50 in Jet Black) for contestants 21 or older.
And while it's not as rare or nearly as expensive secondhand, the Japan-exclusive Gundam Char edition may be the most striking. Like the Final Fantasy variation, this red console and controller were bundled alongside a Game Boy Player.
Tales of Symphonia garnered a similar treatment in 2003 when Nintendo offered the GameCube and Game Boy Player with the title in a mint green bundle. The pastel console was exclusively released in Japan and France with a run of about 10,000 units. This one is more approachable for new collectors; it's much easier to find and goes for no more than $1,500.
According to Consolevariations, some of the rarest unofficial GameCube releases are a pair of airbrushed movie tie-in game consoles originally intended as part of a sweepstakes: one for The Polar Express and the other for The Incredibles. But even with a standard model, your old console could fetch some cash if you no longer use it.

title_fa: Apple’s last-gen Mac Mini with the M4 is $150 off
excerpt_en: Best Buy has a great deal for the rest of the day on the M4 Mac Mini base model that has 16GB RAM and a 256GB SSD. Normally, it doesn’t make a ton of sense to buy the M4 model for its usual $799 price given that the newer, faster M6 version has been available […]
excerpt_fa: Best Buy has a great deal for the rest of the day on the M4 Mac Mini base model that has 16GB RAM and a 256GB SSD. Normally, it doesn’t make a ton of sense to buy the M4 model for its usual $799 price given that the newer, faster M6 version has been available […]
content_en:
Best Buy has a great deal for the rest of the day on the M4 Mac Mini base model that has 16GB RAM and a 256GB SSD. Normally, it doesn’t make a ton of sense to buy the M4 model for its usual $799 price given that the newer, faster M6 version has been available from Amazon for $779.99 (originally $899) for the past couple of weeks. However, at $649 it’s a much more tempting price.
Apple’s last-gen Mac Mini with the M4 is $150 off
At $649, it’s a much better deal. However, the new, faster M6 version is only $130 more.
At $649, it’s a much better deal. However, the new, faster M6 version is only $130 more.
The M4 Mac Mini launched at $599 in 2024, and was an incredible value. Given that this sale price makes it just $50 more than the original price instead of $200, it’s a good time to buy if you want to spend as little as possible on a modern Mac desktop.
Aside from some impressive generational leaps in processing power, you aren’t missing out on a ton by skipping the M6 model and opting for the M4. Their design and ports are nearly identical, and with either model you’ll need to supply your own keyboard, mouse, display, webcam, etc. If you’re on the fence and can’t decide between the M4 and M6 models, I suggest checking out my colleague Antonio’s review of the M6 Mac Mini. The newer model might be well worth the extra $130 cost.
Read our review of the M4 Mac Mini and the M6 Mac Mini
More Verge-approved deals
- Today brought a big discount to LG’s C6 OLEDs lineup, particularly its bigger models. The 55-inch model is $999.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Costco (previously $1,399.99), costing a little less than the 42- and 48-inch configurations. The price hasn’t gone below $1,299.99 before, so it’s a good time to consider an upgrade. The 65-inch model is cheaper than before, too. Previously $1,699.99, but normally selling for $1,500 or so, you can grab the larger version for $1,399.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Costco. If you have a big room and budget, the 77-inch LG C6H that, like the 48-inch version, has a tandem OLED panel that offers more brightness and better colors, is $1,999.99, down from $2,499.99.
- For $499.99, you can grab a 14-inch HP OmniBook 3 during Best Buy’s deal of the day that has a 2K OLED screen, a capable Snapdragon X ARM processor, 16GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD. This seems like a fantastic option for anyone on a budget. Its Snapdragon processor can run most x86 Windows 11 apps without much issue, and it’s just a rarity to get these kinds of specs — from the OLED screen to the RAM amount — at $500. My colleague Antonio reviewed the 16-inch version that cuts some corners in the screen department compared to this 14-inch model.
- It’s time to get spooky if you haven’t already planned your run of games for Halloween. The spectacular Silent Hill 2 remake is down to $21.34 on Steam for PC via Fanatical, a third-party site I’ve shopped from numerous times. If you’re alright with spending more, Resident Evil Requiem is one of Capcom’s several great 2026 games, and it’s $20 off at Amazon on all platforms, costing $49.99.

content_en:
Today, I’m talking with Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who has a lot of thoughts about AI, tech, and privacy.
JB Pritzker thinks AI could help us live to 100 — or threaten us like nukes
The Illinois governor on AI, data centers, privacy, and Trump.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
If you’ve been listening to the show, you know that one of my running theories is that those issues are driving a big and maybe kind of unexpected political realignment — and with the midterms coming up next month, and early voting already underway in a lot of places, the stakes are pretty high right now.
So I asked Gov. Pritzker about all that, and he was surprisingly willing to dive right into the absolute existential weeds of what government is even for. You’ll hear him say — and it’s hard to disagree — that some problems are just collective action problems that require the government to do a lot of work. We can’t solve all these problems one at a time, or even one state at a time. It’s a pretty deep conversation, and we really got into it on a lot of issues.
And of course, I had to ask him: Are the Bears gonna stay in Illinois?
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. Here we go.
Gov. JB Pritzker, you’re the governor of Illinois. Welcome to Decoder.
Thanks, Nilay. Great to be with you.
I am very excited to talk to you. We’re in the heart of midterm season. You are running for reelection. I have to tell you. I have to be very honest with you. I personally feel a lot of pressure in this interview, not only because I’m speaking to a governor, but because I went to school in Chicago. My sister still lives in Chicago. My wife grew up in Illinois. Her entire family is farmers in North Central Illinois. Boy, do I have a list of questions for you. I have to do a good job here.
Well, we’re claiming you. Now that I know all that, we’re claiming you. You’re an Illinoisan.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
I don’t know about that. I grew up in Wisconsin. Here’s my first question for you. I’m a die-hard Packers fan. Are you going to let the Bears move to Indiana?
That is not our intention. We are, in fact, in discussions with the Bears and the NFL about keeping the Bears either in Chicago or in Arlington Heights, but in Illinois.
I’m saying, as a Packers fan, nothing is funnier than the outcome of the Bears moving to Indiana. I just want to put that out there. Openly biased in this case — I own two shares of that stock — but I’m going to make the comparison here. And the reason I started there is not only because I think that’s a funny outcome, although I do, but it feels like we are in the middle of a generational political realignment.
I’m sure you feel that, in this election campaign, the idea of big business and how that should interact with the government, and how the government should be able to push back on big business and not give in to big business. All of that feels up for grabs.
And the comparison I will make in this specific case is your fellow governor, Gavin Newsom, in California. They sued the Ellison family, Paramount, over the Warner Brothers merger. Paramount threatened to leave. They made a lot of noise about Nashville, Texas, Miami, or wherever you make noise about these days, and it feels like Newsom caved. It feels like he pressured his Attorney General, Rob Bonta, to settle that lawsuit and keep them there.
They settled the lawsuit. The next day, the Ellison family is like, “We never... We’re from California. We would never leave.” I see a parallel here with the Bears that is connected to that larger realignment, how government and business should interact. Do you see that parallel? Do you feel that realignment?
Well, what I can tell you is we’re pretty tough negotiators in Chicago and Illinois, and that’s really what we’re in the midst of now with the Bears. But I understand your point about realignment. I mean, there is a generational change, and I think it’s also an attitudinal change about protecting taxpayers, protecting people who frankly are among the most vulnerable to all the technology that’s overtaking people’s lives and invading people’s homes.
And so I do believe that the government has to be more active now and become a fighter for our people and not just a collaborator with business on everything. I’m a businessman, as you know, before I became governor. But I also know that, for the people of Illinois anyway, my job is to protect the working people of this state who often don’t have anybody protecting them except a government that will stand up for them. So that’s kind of the realignment that I see.
And that generational shift, I agree with you. It’s partly a Democratic Party generational shift. Generationally, we’re a little more aggressive. And I’m probably older than the next generation that’s already possibly taking office this November. I’m 61 years old, but I think of myself as having come out of the tech world and as somebody who has been a fighter for progressive values that, yeah, we’ve got to become more aggressive and make sure we’re standing up for our people.
There are two places where I see the realignment in particular. One is data centers, one is privacy, and you just see that as a bipartisan backlash to those things. I would actually add a third, which is antitrust broadly. It’s weird if you go into Silicon Valley. David Sacks is retweeting Lina Khan from the Biden administration talking about whether the AI industry needs an antitrust exemption to manage safety.
They both agree that these companies don’t need antitrust exemptions. They actually should be more competitive. Again, putting that in the context of regulating these companies, thinking about the dynamic...

title_en: What the orange light on your PlayStation 5 is actually telling you
title_fa: What the orange light on your PlayStation 5 is actually telling you
excerpt_en: The PS5 shows a variety of light colors to indicate its status, and orange thankfully isn't the alert you might expect from that color.
excerpt_fa: The PS5 shows a variety of light colors to indicate its status, and orange thankfully isn't the alert you might expect from that color.
content_en:
What the orange light on your PlayStation 5 is actually telling you
Unlike many orange icons and lights, this one isn't a warning sign.
Orange isn't the most reassuring color to see displayed on a device. It's something that can trigger a visceral reaction of panic, given its use for elements like check engine lights in a car and faulty power supplies for past consoles. Thankfully, on a PlayStation 5 it's nothing to worry about; it just means the console has entered Rest Mode. An unrelated orange light on your PS5 controller below the PS button indicates that your mic is muted — press that button to unmute.
Rest Mode is an incredibly handy feature that saves power while still allowing your console to perform basic tasks. Depending on your PS5's settings, it can work to charge your controllers and download games while consuming only a few watts. Entering Rest Mode after a set period of inactivity is part of the console's factory settings, but you can easily adjust this or disable it entirely.
To enter Rest Mode when you're done playing, simply press the power button on the front of the console for a moment. Alternatively, hit the PS button on your controller to open the control center, then go to Power > Enter Rest Mode. Never unplug your PS5 when you see the orange light, as it's not fully powered off in that state. Select Turn Off PS5 from the Power menu and wait for the system lights to go out before unplugging it.
How to change your PlayStation 5's Rest Mode settings
If your PS5 is entering Rest Mode from inactivity faster than you want, you can change the timer for this in its settings:
-
From the home screen, select Settings at the top-right.
-
Select System, then Power Saving.
-
Select Set Time Until PS5 Enters Rest Mode.
From here, you can set how long the console will remain inactive before entering Rest Mode, with separate settings for media playback and while playing games. If you'd like, you can also choose to have your PS5 never enter Rest Mode, even after prolonged inactivity.
Also in the Power Saving section of system settings, select Features Available in Rest Mode to determine how much your PS5 will do while resting. This is where you can choose to power the USB ports, update games, upload saves to the cloud or play games remotely using a PlayStation Portal or other device via remote play.
PlayStation 5 hardware warning signs
While an orange light on your PS5 is nothing to worry about, there are other signs when your console is having trouble and might need repair. The console has been around for nearly six years, and there's no clear timeline for how long a PS5 should be expected to last. Sony's track record of continuing to support the PS4 with updates bodes well for the firmware side as the PS5 gets on in years, but it's smart to keep an eye on your hardware. Considering how the PS5 has gone up in price since release, the earlier you can address and fix problems (and in turn avoid having to purchase a new console), the better.
One of the most common PS5 issues is overheating, which can either be a product of the environment it's in (like blocked or dusty exhaust vents) or the cooling system naturally degrading over time. Possible signs of overheating include the console shutting down unexpectedly, extremely hot or loud air flow coming from its vents or even an on-screen warning about the console's temperature. If it continues to be a problem even after you've cleaned out dust and placed it in a well-ventilated area, it might be worth bringing it to a professional to have the thermal paste replaced. Repeated overheating can damage internal components and lead to more problems later on.
Another one of the most frequent PS5 problems is GPU failure, which presents as visual glitches like screen flickering, static or multicolored lines. These can also be caused by HDMI issues, however, so it's worth trying another high-quality HDMI cable and HDMI port on your TV before assuming your GPU is failing. Plugging your PS5 into another monitor or TV is also a good step to rule out the display as the root cause.
If problems persist, it's likely that your GPU is failing. Unfortunately, because of the specific parts a PS5 uses, the solution for this is to either send the console to Sony for repair or take it to a specialized repair shop.

title_en: Don't throw away your old graphics card — here's what you can do with it
title_fa: Don't throw away your old graphics card — here's what you can do with it
excerpt_en: An old GPU has lots of potential for a second life, from adding more horsepower to your current machine to crafting a purpose-built second one.
excerpt_fa: An old GPU has lots of potential for a second life, from adding more horsepower to your current machine to crafting a purpose-built second one.
content_en:
Don't throw away your old graphics card — here's what you can do with it
Some older graphics cards are still worth almost as much as they initially cost, so don’t waste their potential.
Especially in the current climate, you probably don't have to be told that throwing away your old graphics card is a bad idea. They're expensive, and you can repurpose your prior one after you upgrade. Every three to five years is a common cadence for GPU upgrades, so it's important to think about what happens to your investment when the next cycle comes around.
The most popular card in the latest Steam hardware survey is the Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070, which is installed in 6.15 percent of surveyed systems. It launched at $549 and can now cost more than $800 because of memory and silicon price inflation. Increased prices mean more people will use their GPUs for longer, which may stretch the typical upgrade cycle.
Just because you've outgrown your graphics card doesn't mean everyone else has, so selling your old GPU to get some value back is a good option. An eBay search at the time of writing shows some used RTX 3060s selling for almost as much as they originally cost. Even the 10-year-old $249 GTX 1060 is typically listed at $50 to $100 in good condition, though these are always subject to fluctuation.
What to do with an old graphics card
You can repurpose your old graphics card by installing it into your home media server to handle hardware-accelerated video encoding and decoding using Nvidia's NVENC or AMD's AMF. Both Jellyfin and Plex support hardware-accelerated streaming, so your old GPU can gain new life converting video codecs in real time to offload tasks from the processor.
Alternatively, you can build a PC to connect to your TV that also runs as a gaming console. You don't need state-of-the-art performance for light indie games or emulation, and sometimes older hardware can work better with past releases designed for older standards. Use it to run titles built using legacy code libraries, DirectX 9-era games, or to gain extra HDMI/DisplayPort connections to drive additional displays.
Using the card in a spare slot in your main PC to run legacy software may also work, if you have enough power and ventilation. However, there are caveats to running two GPUs in one chassis. You'll need a power supply and motherboard capable of handling dual GPUs and may bump into PCIe lane limits. If your processor uses lane splitting, a second card can degrade the performance of your primary GPU, which is a problem. Check your motherboard manual to see how it handles different expansion slots before you commit resources to this project.
Even more: streaming, gaming, encoding and AI
Gamers have even more options to repurpose an old GPU. Try running Lossless Scaling ($6.99 on Steam) on your old card as second-fiddle support for your new one, or use it to capture in-game video while the primary GPU runs the game. You might build a separate PC for capturing video streams, or as a video encoding and editing rig handling tasks in DaVinci Resolve or Blender. It can even be a good option for running local AI workloads, given how heavily those rely on VRAM.
Holding onto the video card to have a spare in case one fails isn't a bad idea if you have no other use in mind. Just be aware the money you could make selling it will drop over time, and remember to store it safely in an antistatic bag.
Finally, a word about recycling: even if you plan to get rid of it, you shouldn't throw electronics out with the trash. Companies that do e-waste recycling will take your old card to break it down. Even if your old card is irreparable, the gold, copper and aluminum it contains will have value somewhere, so recycling it is way better than chucking electronics into a landfill.

title_en: Apple updates guidelines to ban nudify apps masquerading as regular apps to pass review
title_fa: Apple updates guidelines to ban nudify apps masquerading as regular apps to pass review
excerpt_en: The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content.
excerpt_fa: The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content.
content_en:
Apple tightened its developer guidelines over the weekend to ban apps that use AI to create offensive content, as well as those that masquerade as regular apps to pass the App Store review process and then turn into nudify apps, or surface those features prominently.
The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content.
“Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as ‘nudification’ — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch,” the company said in a blog post.
Apple said that it will remove apps that add features not present in the version submitted for App Store review.
The iPhone maker has also updated the language in its legal section to reinforce that it will bar apps promoting human trafficking and exploitation of children.
Apple said last year its review process blocked over 150,000 apps from reaching users and removed 193,000 developer accounts due to fraud and abuse.
In July, the city of San Francisco ordered both Apple and Google to clean up and delete nudification apps from their app stores. City Attorney David Chiu accused the companies of profiting from these apps through store fees. And in April, a Tech Transparency Project report indicated that both tech giants’ stores hosted multiple nudify apps, some of which were rated as suitable for minors.
